title: Auditory Perception and Cognitive Performance
authors: Angélique A. Scharine et al., null
review_question: What are the mechanisms, characteristics, and effects of auditory perception on cognitive performance, including sound detection, discrimination, loudness, pitch, timbre, spatial perception, speech communication, and the impact of hearing loss?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Not specified, this is a narrative review summarizing existing knowledge.

findings.antecedent: Auditory sensation (basic physical characteristics of sound)
findings.quote: Auditory sensation does not involve sound recognition, which requires a higher level of cognitive processing of the auditory stimuli. This higher level processing forms a conceptual interpretation of the auditory stimulus and is referred to as auditory perception.

findings.antecedent: Linear changes in acoustic stimulation
findings.source: Page 2, Sound Pressure and Sound Pressure Level section
findings.quote: human auditory perception is far from linear. Human perception is relative by nature and logarithmic in general, i.e., linear changes in the amount of stimulation cause logarithmic changes in human perception

findings.antecedent: Hearing threshold
findings.quote: Normal daily variability of the threshold of hearing can be assumed to be 6 dB or less.

findings.antecedent: Listener's familiarity, interest, attention, experience (with stimuli/task)
findings.quote: The cognitive thresholds can be made close to the physiological thresholds by an appropriate amount and type of training

findings.antecedent: Binaural listening (compared to monaural, with similar ear sensitivity)
findings.quote: The binaural thresholds of hearing shown in Figure 11-1 and Table 11-1 are approximately 2 dB lower than the corresponding monaural thresholds if both ears have similar sensitivity

findings.antecedent: Sound frequency (1.5 to 6 kHz range, especially 3.0 to 4.0 kHz)
findings.quote: the auditory system is especially sensitive to sound energy in the 1.5 to 6 kHz range with the most sensitive region being in the 3.0 to 4.0 kHz range

findings.antecedent: Sound presentation method (free-field MAF vs. earphone MAP)
findings.quote: The average difference between both thresholds is in the order of 6 dB to 10 dB

findings.antecedent: Noisy environment (for talker)
findings.consequent: Talker's voice (vowel duration, intensity) and Speech intelligibility
findings.quote: The Lombard effect (Lombard, 1911) is a phenomenon in which a talker alters his or her voice in noisy environments. Generally, there is an increase in vowel duration and voice intensity

findings.antecedent: Speech-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)
findings.source: Page 56, Speech perception and environment section
findings.quote: Good understanding of speech requires high SNRs in the order of 15 to 30 dB. Smaller SNRs lead to reduced speech intelligibility scores.

findings.antecedent: Type of background noise (random, unpredictable, speech-like)
findings.source: Page 56, Speech perception and environment section
findings.quote: random, unpredictable noise, or noise where the temporal and spectral characteristics are similar to that of speech, can add informational masking to the energetic masking. Therefore, the most efficient masker of speech is other speech

findings.antecedent: Reverberation (high decay time, e.g., >5 seconds)
findings.source: Page 56, Speech perception and environment section
findings.quote: Reverberation consists of multiple reflections of the sound that mask the direct sound... can make normal speech communication in these spaces virtually impossible.

findings.antecedent: Spatial separation of speech source and noise source
findings.source: Page 57, Speech perception and environment section
findings.quote: If the two signals are separated in space, binaural cues can be used to separate the two locations, and the listener can selectively attend to the target speech signal.

findings.antecedent: Presence of one's own name in background noise
findings.source: Page 57, Speech perception and environment section
findings.quote: The most notable of these is known as the “cocktail party phenomenon” where the listener embedded in “party noise” can clearly hear his or her own name when spoken, even though other speech may not be audible

findings.antecedent: Speech material complexity, contextual information, redundancy
findings.quote: Speech intelligibility performance generally improves as the material becomes more complex and contains more contextual information and higher degree of redundancy

findings.antecedent: Speech test type (open set vs. closed set, meaningless vs. meaningful items)
findings.quote: Usually, open set tests are more difficult then closed set tests, and tests using meaningless syllables or sentences are more difficult than tests using meaningful items.

findings.antecedent: Talker characteristics (clear speech, female voice)
findings.quote: A trained talker such as radio announcer who speaks clearly will be more intelligible than a talker using normal conversational speech.

findings.antecedent: Listener characteristics (training, hearing sensitivity)
findings.quote: Trained listeners who are familiar with the test and the speech material to be tested will perform best and have the most reliable scores

findings.antecedent: Binaural listening
findings.quote: binaural listening allows the listener to utilize the better ear advantage... Second, the listener can use spatial localization cues

findings.antecedent: Auditory cues (loudness, timbre, reverberance/liveness, motion parallax)
findings.quote: These cues, called distance cues or range cues, depend on the specific environment but in general include: (a) sound loudness, (b) spectral changes, (c) space reverberance (liveness), and (c) motion parallax.

findings.antecedent: Actual distance to sound source
findings.quote: In general, people underestimate the distance to the sound source in an exponential manner – the larger the distance to the sound source the larger relative error

findings.antecedent: Acoustic space characteristics (ambience, reverberance, warmth, intimacy, panorama, perspective)
findings.quote: Spaciousness embraces such sensations as ambience... reverberance or liveness... warmth... intimacy, panorama, perspective, and many others.

findings.antecedent: Auditory personal space (radius)
findings.quote: the distance of one meter (3.28 feet) defines a typical conversational situation and serves as a good estimate of the radius of the auditory personal space.

findings.antecedent: Perceived auditory distance (different from 1 to 1.5 m for voice communication)
findings.quote: If the perceived auditory distance to another talker in an audio channel is quite different from 1 to 1.5 m, such voice communication will distract the operator, increase the workload, and increase the overall level of anxiety.

findings.antecedent: Hearing loss
findings.quote: Hearing loss is a decreased ability to perceive sound due to an abnormality in the hearing mechanism... Hearing loss can affect not only the individual's ability to hear the surrounding environment but also the clarity of speech perception.

findings.antecedent: Anomalies in outer ear (causing conductive hearing loss)
findings.quote: The resonance of the pinna and the outer ear canal is between 2 to 7 kHz, which enhances the ability of the listener to localize and perceive their acoustic space... anomalies in the outer can impede the listener's ability to localize.

findings.antecedent: Sensorineural hearing loss (cochlear/neural abnormality)
findings.quote: Sensorineural hearing loss is characterized by irreversible damage that distorts auditory perception.

findings.antecedent: Age (7th decade, aging women)
findings.consequent: Hearing loss (high-frequency, lower frequencies for aging women)
findings.quote: Age-related hearing loss is most commonly seen in the 7th decade of life, with the basal region of the cochlea being most affected

findings.antecedent: Speech intelligibility (high and similar)
findings.quote: when the compared samples of speech have the same, or very similar, and relatively high speech intelligibility, these samples may still greatly differ in speech quality and these differences may be reliably assessed by the listeners.

findings.antecedent: Speech quality
findings.quote: In general, the higher speech quality, the greater satisfaction and listening comfort of the listener.

findings.antecedent: Sound frequency, temporal envelope, spectral characteristics, and duration
findings.quote: Loudness depends primarily upon the sound pressure of the stimulus but also depends upon its frequency, temporal envelope, spectral characteristics, and duration

findings.antecedent: Sound pressure level (high vs. low intensity)
findings.consequent: Ear sensitivity to intensity fluctuations as a function of frequency
findings.quote: at high intensity levels the ear is less sensitive to fluctuations in intensity as a function of frequency than at low intensity levels.

findings.antecedent: Speech in quiet or low levels of background noise
findings.source: Page 19, Most comfortable loudness level section
findings.quote: For most listeners the MCL for listening to speech in quiet or low levels of background noise is approximately 60 to 65 dB SPL

findings.antecedent: Listening level (at MCL vs. other levels)
findings.source: Page 19, Most comfortable loudness level section
findings.quote: listening to sound at the MCL results in the best and most consistent human performance. Listening at levels other than the MCL also demands increased attention resources and causes the listener to become fatigued more rapidly.

findings.antecedent: Background noise level (up to 40 dB SPL vs. above 40 dB SPL)
findings.source: Page 20, Most comfortable loudness level section
findings.quote: noise levels up to 40 dB SPL have a negligible effect on the MCL for speech. Above this noise level, the MCL for speech appears to be the level that results in a SNR of approximately 15 dB.

findings.antecedent: Very high listening level (above 85 phons)
findings.consequent: Listening experience (exciting), perceived sound image clarity, fatigue
findings.source: Page 20, Most comfortable loudness level section
findings.quote: The selection of a very high listening level (above 85 phons) frequently makes the listening experience more exciting... However, it also makes the perceived sound image less clear... and is more tiring

findings.antecedent: Sound duration (shorter than critical duration, e.g., 200-300 ms)
findings.quote: For sounds shorter than critical duration, the loudness of sound increases with sound duration

findings.antecedent: Prolonged auditory stimulation; decreasing stimulus level; increasing frequency
findings.source: Page 24, Auditory adaptation and fatigue section
findings.quote: if the auditory stimulus acts for a prolonged period of time, the sensation of loudness slightly decreases... The amount of adaptation is dependent on the frequency, level and duration of the auditory stimulus and increases with decreasing level of the stimulus and increasing frequency

findings.antecedent: Auditory stimulation (exceeding 70 dB SPL)
findings.source: Page 24, Auditory adaptation and fatigue section
findings.quote: Fatigue is a loss of sensitivity as a result of auditory stimulation, manifesting itself as a temporary shift in the auditory threshold after termination of the stimulus... appears gradually for sounds exceeding 70 dB SPL.

findings.antecedent: Excessive/recurring acoustic trauma (continuous noise > 85 dB SPL, impulse noise > 140 dB)
findings.source: Page 25, Auditory adaptation and fatigue section
findings.quote: Exposure to recurring or extreme acoustic trauma can result in permanent hearing loss.

findings.antecedent: Masker intensity (relative to target sound)
findings.quote: More intense sounds mask less intense sounds.

findings.antecedent: Masker characteristics (energetic vs. informational)
findings.consequent: Masking mechanism (peripheral vs. central auditory nervous system)
findings.quote: Energetic masking is peripheral masking caused by the overlap of the excitation patterns... Informational masking is related to non-energetic characteristics of the masker and may take place even if there is no overlap

findings.antecedent: Masker intensity (10 dB increase)
findings.quote: the masked threshold increases about 10 dB for every 10 dB increase in masker.

findings.antecedent: Frequency (above 500 Hz)
findings.quote: masked threshold curves produced by white noise are fairly independent of frequency up to about 500 Hz and then increase with frequency at a rate of approximately 3 dB/octave (10 dB/decade).

findings.antecedent: Masker intensity
findings.quote: the upward spread of masking is much greater than the downward spread of masking, and this disproportional growth increases with the increase in the intensity of the masker.

findings.antecedent: Narrowband masker bandwidth (up to critical band)
findings.quote: As the bandwidth of the narrowband masker increases, its masking effectiveness increases until its bandwidth exceeds the limits of the critical band

findings.antecedent: Signal energy in several critical bands (complex tone)
findings.quote: simultaneous presence of signal energy in several critical bands aids signal detection.

findings.antecedent: Time difference between masker offset and target onset (longer than 200 ms)
findings.quote: Little masking occurs for times longer than 200 ms

findings.antecedent: Temporal masking (e.g., strong vowel masking weak consonant)
findings.quote: Temporal masking, and especially forward masking, plays an important role in auditory perception because it degrades temporal cues in perceived stimuli.

findings.antecedent: Masker-target similarity; Masker variability/uncertainty
findings.quote: Two main causes of informational masking are similarity between the masker and the target sound and the variability (uncertainty) of the masker

findings.antecedent: Age
findings.quote: the effectiveness of informational masking increases with age even in people with otologically normal hearing.

findings.antecedent: Critical band
findings.quote: a CB takes a relatively constant length of 1.3 mm along the basilar membrane and can be used as a unit of frequency along the basilar membrane. It also corresponds to about 1300 neurons in the cochlea

findings.antecedent: Frequency
findings.quote: Pitch is the perceptual correlate of frequency. It is a sensation that the sound has a specific physical frequency.

findings.antecedent: Spectral complexity, intensity (for complex tones)
findings.quote: pitch and frequency are not related in a simple one-to-one manner but depend on other physical properties of the stimulus, such as spectral complexity and intensity.

findings.antecedent: Sounds separated by one or more octaves
findings.quote: all sounds that are separated by one or more octaves fuse together very well and are sometimes very hard to differentiate from one another

findings.antecedent: Group of pure tones (equally spaced in frequency)
findings.quote: If a group of pure tones, equally spaced in frequency are presented together, a pitch corresponding to the common frequency distance between the individual components will be heard.

findings.antecedent: Orderly pattern of harmonics; narrow band of frequencies
findings.quote: sounds with an orderly pattern of harmonics had the strongest pitch, as well as those containing a narrow band of frequencies.

findings.antecedent: Sound intensity (increased, for higher/lower frequencies)
findings.quote: for tones of higher frequencies, increased sound intensity produces an increase in pitch. Conversely, for tones of lower frequencies, increased sound intensity produces a decrease in pitch.

findings.antecedent: Rising sound intensity (dynamic change)
findings.quote: listeners perceived the rising sound intensity as an upward shift in pitch.

findings.antecedent: Frequency components within same critical band (small frequency difference)
findings.consequent: Phase changes, pitch value, pitch clarity
findings.quote: if two frequency components... fall into the same critical band and their difference in frequency is rather small, the changes in their phase relationship are audible and affect both pitch value and pitch clarity

findings.antecedent: Timbre (spectral and temporal envelope)
findings.consequent: Sound source identification, auditory image storage
findings.source: Page 44, Timbre and pattern recognition section
findings.quote: timbre is the perceptual property of sound that reflects unique properties of the sound and its sound source... and facilitates identification and storage of auditory images.

findings.antecedent: Continuous sound onset
findings.source: Page 45, Timbre and pattern recognition section
findings.quote: it takes at least 60 ms to recognize the timbre of continuous sound after its onset.

findings.antecedent: Binaural cues (ITD, ILD)
findings.consequent: Sound localization (left-right lateralization, front-back differentiation, elevation information)
findings.source: Page 70, Localization and monaural cues section
findings.quote: Binaural cues allow effective left-right lateralization, but they have two major limitations. First, binaural cues do not differentiate between sound arriving from the front or the rear of the head... Second, binaural cues do not provide any information about sound source elevation.

findings.antecedent: Monaural cues (spectral localization cues from pinnae/shoulders)
findings.source: Page 70, Localization and monaural cues section
findings.quote: Monaural cues are the primary cues allowing sound source localization in the vertical place and along the front-back axis.

findings.antecedent: Head movement (small, left-right, vertical)
findings.quote: Small movements of the head from the left to the right will quickly clarify whether the sound is in the front or rear hemisphere. Vertical movements give salient elevation information

findings.antecedent: Successively received similar sounds (second delayed 30-40ms, second not >10dB more intense than first)
findings.quote: the perception of the second of two successively received similar sounds is suppressed if the second sound is delayed up to about 30 to 40 ms, and its intensity does not exceed the intensity of the first sound by more than 10 dB.

findings.antecedent: Two arriving sounds (different locations, fused image)
findings.quote: If the locations of the two arriving sounds differ, the perceived location of the fused click image is largely determined by the location of the first click.

synthesis_conclusions: Auditory perception involves higher-level cognitive processing beyond basic sensation, influenced by logarithmic scaling of physical stimuli.
Hearing thresholds exhibit both daily and inter-subject variability, with binaural listening offering a 2 dB advantage over monaural listening.
The auditory system is most sensitive to sound energy in the 1.5 to 6 kHz range, particularly 3.0 to 4.0 kHz.
The Lombard effect demonstrates that talkers alter their voice (increased vowel duration and intensity) in noisy environments, which improves speech intelligibility.

Speech intelligibility is highly dependent on SNR (15-30 dB for good understanding), type of background noise (informational maskers like other speech are most efficient), and reverberation (high decay times can make communication impossible).
Spatial separation of speech and noise sources, as well as the 'cocktail party phenomenon' (detection of one's own name), enhance speech intelligibility and attention.
Speech intelligibility improves with more complex, contextual, and redundant speech material, but is negatively impacted by open-set or meaningless test materials.
Talker characteristics (clear speech, female voice) and listener characteristics (training, hearing sensitivity) significantly influence speech intelligibility.
Auditory distance perception relies on cues such as loudness, timbre, reverberance/liveness, and motion parallax, but humans generally underestimate distance exponentially.
Spaciousness is a multidimensional sensation encompassing ambience, reverberance, warmth, intimacy, panorama, and perspective, reflecting the acoustic environment.
Auditory personal space, typically around 1 meter for conversational situations, is crucial for communication; deviations from this distance can increase operator distraction, workload, and anxiety.
Hearing loss, particularly sensorineural loss, decreases speech clarity and distorts auditory perception, with outer ear anomalies also impeding sound localization.
Age-related hearing loss primarily affects high frequencies, with specific patterns differing between genders.
Speech quality can be reliably assessed when speech intelligibility is high and similar, and higher speech quality generally correlates with greater listener satisfaction and comfort.

Perceived loudness is influenced by sound pressure, frequency, temporal envelope, spectral characteristics, and duration, with ear sensitivity to intensity fluctuations decreasing at high intensity levels.
The Most Comfortable Loudness (MCL) for speech is around 60-65 dB SPL, and listening at MCL optimizes human performance while reducing attention demands and fatigue.

Loudness adaptation occurs with prolonged stimulation, increasing with decreasing stimulus level and increasing frequency, while auditory fatigue (TTS) results from excessive noise exposure (>70 dB SPL) and can lead to permanent hearing loss (>85 dB SPL continuous, >140 dB impulse).
Masking effects are stronger with higher masker intensity, extend further into high frequencies (upward spread), and are most effective when masker bandwidth is within the critical band.
Informational masking is caused by masker-target similarity and masker uncertainty, and its effectiveness increases with age.
The critical band is a fundamental unit of auditory processing, corresponding to a constant length on the basilar membrane and a specific number of neurons.

Pitch is the perceptual correlate of frequency, but for complex tones, it also depends on spectral complexity and intensity; sounds separated by octaves tend to fuse, and residual pitch can be perceived from equally spaced pure tones.

Pitch strength is enhanced by orderly harmonic patterns and narrow frequency bands, and perceived pitch can be influenced by sound intensity (increasing for higher frequencies, decreasing for lower frequencies).
The 'Doppler illusion' demonstrates that rising sound intensity can be perceived as an upward pitch shift, highlighting the integral perception of auditory dimensions.
Phase changes are audible and affect pitch only when frequency components fall within the same critical band with small frequency differences.
Timbre, defined by spectral and temporal envelopes, is crucial for sound source identification and auditory image storage, with recognition taking at least 60 ms.

Binaural cues (ITD, ILD) are effective for left-right lateralization but limited for front-back differentiation and elevation, which are primarily resolved by monaural spectral cues from the pinnae and shoulders.
Head movements significantly clarify sound localization, especially for front-back and elevation cues.

The precedence effect suppresses the perception of a delayed second sound if it is similar and within certain intensity and time parameters (e.g., 30-40 ms delay, second sound not >10 dB more intense), with the perceived location of fused sounds determined by the first sound's location.
evidence_gaps: Environmental sound research is still in its beginning stages, with few quantitative studies on thresholds for various environmental and man-made sounds.
There is no strict standard accepted for how to calculate bilateral Pure Tone Average (PTA) for binaural hearing loss.
The physiological mechanism responsible for auditory adaptation is still not clear.
The exact physiologic mechanism of the binaural masking level difference (MLD) is still unknown.
It is still unclear what the shape of the critical band filters is and whether it depends on sound intensity.
The mel scale has been criticized for being counterintuitive and counterproductive for different octaves to have different perceptual size.
The physiologic basis of backward masking is still largely unknown.
There are few studies reporting thresholds of hearing for various environmental and man-made sounds.
The specific methodology of data collection for differential thresholds needs to be known to interpret published values of DLs.
The physiologic mechanisms behind the growth of the loudness function are not entirely clear.
There is still a debate in the literature regarding the difference between monaural and binaural loudness.
The physiologic mechanism responsible for auditory adaptation is still not clear.
To date, no official binaural version of speech intelligibility indexes (AI/STI) exists.

Speech intelligibility measures (perceptual and objective) are not truly able to measure the degree to which speech communication occurs beyond phoneme/syllable recognition, lacking higher-order comprehension and contextual information.
The multidimensional character of timbre is not well-described by a global assessment alone, and there is a need for universally accepted, limited timbre terminology.
It is still unclear what the shape of the critical band filters is and whether it depends on sound intensity.

The perception of phase and polarity has been a long-debated topic in audition, with some studies showing sensitivity to phase changes even when frequency components are separated by more than one critical band, challenging the view of the auditory system as a power detector.
The lack of familiarity with specific auditory stimuli is frequently reported as a secondary reason for front-back confusions and poor localization in the vertical plane.
risk_of_bias_assessment: Not applicable for a narrative review.
publication_bias: Not applicable for a narrative review.
limitations: The chapter primarily summarizes existing knowledge and does not present new empirical data or a systematic review methodology.
Many reported values (e.g., thresholds, DLs) are averages and can vary significantly with individual differences, stimulus characteristics, and environmental conditions.
The applicability of some concepts (e.g., equal-loudness contours for noises, mel scale for music/speech) is limited or debated.
Speech intelligibility metrics (AI, STI) have limitations in accounting for temporal distortion, non-linear effects, and spatial arrangement of sound sources.
The terminology used in speech tests and assessments often lacks discipline, leading to potential misinterpretation.
The chapter acknowledges that some areas, like environmental sound research, are still in early stages with limited quantitative data.
